topic: 10 Most Daring Special Forces Raids of World War Two
hook: Ten raids. Ten missions that should have been impossible. Most of them were planned in months. Some in days. Almost all of them sent men into territory they were not expected to leave.
narration:
Ten raids. Ten missions that should have been impossible. Most of them were planned in months. Some in days. Almost all of them sent men into territory they were not expected to leave.

This is not a list of the biggest battles of the Second World War. It is not a list of the bloodiest. It is a list of the ten times a small group of soldiers went somewhere a whole army could not. Did something a whole army could not do. And changed the course of the war from the inside.

You will hear about a fortress that fell in twenty hours to eighty-five men. A canoe raid that started with twelve and came back with two. A general saved from a mountaintop hotel by ten silent gliders. A radar set carried back across the English Channel in a paratrooper's pocket. A prison camp emptied of more than two thousand civilians on the morning they were going to be executed.

Some of these raids you have heard of. The ones you have not are often the ones the men who planned them counted as the most extraordinary. We are going to count down from ten to one.

Before we begin, if you find these stories worth your time, subscribe to the channel. We tell one of these every week, sourced from primary archives. That subscribe button is the only reason we can keep going.

Number ten. Operation Chastise. Germany. May the sixteenth, nineteen forty-three.

The Ruhr Valley is the industrial heart of the Third Reich. Its factories run on water and electricity, and the water and the electricity come from a chain of dams. The British know that if they can break the dams, they can cripple German war production for months. The problem is the dams are too big to bomb. Conventional bombs slide down their concrete faces and explode harmlessly in the water below.

So a British engineer named Barnes Wallis builds a different kind of bomb. A drum-shaped four-thousand-pound charge that, if dropped at exactly two hundred and thirty-two miles an hour, from exactly sixty feet above the water, will skip across the surface of the reservoir like a stone, hit the dam wall, sink to a precise depth, and detonate.

To deliver it, the Royal Air Force creates a single squadron. Number six-one-seven, formed in March nineteen forty-three for one mission. Their commander is a twenty-four-year-old wing commander named Guy Gibson.

On the night of May the sixteenth, nineteen Lancaster bombers take off from Lincolnshire. They fly at fifty feet to stay below German radar. When they reach the Möhne dam, they line up one by one in the moonlight, full throttle, sixty feet above the water, while German flak guns fire down on them from the dam itself.

The Möhne breaks. Then the Eder. A wall of water more than thirty feet high tears down the valleys behind them, washing away factories, power stations, and twelve hundred lives.

Eight of the nineteen Lancasters do not come home. Fifty-three of the one hundred and thirty-three crew die in a single night.

Guy Gibson is awarded the Victoria Cross. He is killed on another raid sixteen months later. He is twenty-six years old.

But Operation Chastise is only number ten. Because the next raid took a fortress no army had ever taken.

Number nine. Fort Eben-Emael. Belgium. May the tenth, nineteen forty.

If you wanted to invade France in nineteen forty, you had to go through Belgium. If you wanted to go through Belgium, you had to get past Fort Eben-Emael. It is the largest fortress in the world. Six hundred meters long. Seventeen retractable gun cupolas. Twelve hundred men inside, dug into limestone fifty meters underground. The Belgian army considers it impregnable. They estimate that any attacker would need a week of artillery and infantry to reduce it.

The Germans take it in twenty hours. With eighty-five men.

Hitler's personal pilot, Hanna Reitsch, has told him that combat gliders are nearly silent in flight. Belgian listening posts use sound, not radar, to detect aircraft. So at dawn on May the tenth, eleven gliders cast off from their tow planes high over the Dutch border and slide downward in total silence toward the roof of Fort Eben-Emael.

Nine of them land directly on top of the fort. The men inside are paratroopers from a unit called Sturmgruppe Granit, commanded by a lieutenant named Rudolf Witzig. They are carrying a weapon the world has never seen used in battle. Shaped-charge demolition kits. They place these against the steel cupolas of the fort's gun turrets and detonate them. The shaped charges burn through the steel and kill the gun crews inside.

Within fifteen minutes, the Belgians have lost most of their main armament. The Germans hold the roof. They cannot get in, but the Belgians cannot get out, and the Belgian guns can no longer fire on the bridges over the Albert Canal that the rest of the German army needs to cross.

By the next morning, the Belgian commander surrenders. Six Germans are dead. Seven hundred and eighty Belgians march out of the fort with their hands held high.

The world's first glider-borne assault. The blueprint every airborne unit on Earth would copy for the next eighty years. But the next raid proved a small force could rescue the people no one else could reach.

Number eight. The Cabanatuan raid. The Philippines. January the thirtieth, nineteen forty-five. Pronounced Kah-bah-na-TOO-an.

When the Japanese invaded the Philippines in nineteen forty-two, they took twenty-two thousand American and Filipino prisoners. Most were marched up the Bataan Peninsula. Many died on the way. The survivors were pushed through a network of camps until, by January nineteen forty-five, only the worst of them remained, held in a camp called Cabanatuan, sixty miles behind Japanese lines.

There are five hundred and eleven men inside. Most of them are skeletons. Many have been imprisoned for almost three years. American intelligence has just learned that the Japanese army is now massacring its prisoners as it retreats. Two weeks earlier, on the island of Palawan, Japanese guards burned one hundred and fifty American prisoners alive in their own air-raid shelters. The men of Cabanatuan are next.

The Sixth Ranger Battalion is given the mission. One hundred and twenty-one Rangers, supported by two hundred Filipino guerrillas under Captains Juan Pajota and Eduardo Joson. They have to march thirty miles through Japanese-held territory, on foot, without being seen. They have to cross a major road being used by retreating Japanese tanks. They have to hit the camp at exactly the right moment. And they have to get the prisoners, most of whom cannot walk, back across thirty miles of open countryside before sunrise.

The attack opens at seven forty-five in the evening. A single American P-Sixty-One Black Widow night fighter buzzes the camp from above to distract the guards while the Rangers crawl through the grass to the wire.

Thirty seconds. That is how long the firefight inside the camp lasts before every Japanese guard is dead.

The Rangers carry the prisoners out. Filipino farmers bring carabao carts to carry the weakest. By dawn, every one of the five hundred and eleven prisoners is behind American lines. Two Rangers killed. Two Filipino guerrillas killed. Zero prisoners left behind.

But before any rescue raid of this kind was possible, the British had to prove that a tiny force could capture something the Germans guarded as if their lives depended on it.

Number seven. Operation Biting. France. The night of February the twenty-seventh, nineteen forty-two.

By early nineteen forty-two, British bomber losses over Germany are catastrophic. The reason is a new German radar called the Würzburg. Pronounced VURTZ-burg. A dish-shaped antenna ten feet across that can guide night fighters straight to a bomber stream from sixty miles away. The British know it exists. They know roughly how it looks. They cannot understand how it works. And they cannot afford to keep losing aircraft until they do.

A reconnaissance Spitfire takes a photograph of one of these radar sets. It is sitting on a clifftop above a quiet village in Normandy called Bruneval. The British decide that the only way to learn how the Würzburg works is to steal one.

A force is assembled. One hundred and twenty paratroopers of C Company, the Second Parachute Battalion, under a major named John Frost. With them is a flight sergeant named Charles Cox, a radio engineer who has volunteered for an operation he has not been told the details of. Cox has never jumped out of an aeroplane. He has never been in combat. His job is to take the radar apart in the dark, in the snow, while German soldiers shoot at him.

On the night of February the twenty-seventh, twelve Whitley bombers drop the company over Normandy. Frost's men land in the snow, kill the German guards on the radar position in less than five minutes, and set up a perimeter. While they hold off counter-attacking infantry, Cox climbs up to the dish, traces every cable, photographs every component, and unbolts the parts the engineers in London want.

He takes the radar's transmitter. The receiver. The display unit. He drops them into a haversack and crawls down to the beach, where Royal Navy landing craft have come in to extract the force.

Three British dead. Six wounded. One Würzburg radar, in pieces, in a Royal Navy gunboat heading back to Portsmouth.

What the British scientists learn from those parts allows them to jam the Würzburg, defeat it, and plan the air operations of D-Day around it. A clifftop raid by one hundred and twenty men changes the air war.

But the Bruneval raid succeeded because the men got in and out alive. The next raid did not. And the men who did not come back changed the war anyway.

Number six. Operation Frankton. France. December the seventh, nineteen forty-two.

Bordeaux is the second-largest port in France. The Germans use it to ship rubber, tin, tungsten, and other strategic cargoes from Japan and the Far East back to Europe. It is one hundred miles inland, up the heavily defended Gironde estuary. A bombing raid would kill thousands of French civilians. A commando landing would be cut to pieces before it reached the docks. So in late nineteen forty-two, Combined Operations approves the most improbable plan of the war.

Twelve Royal Marines are going to paddle to Bordeaux. In canoes. From a submarine. At night. Six wood-and-canvas kayaks, two men each, each carrying eight limpet mines. They will paddle one hundred miles up the estuary in five nights. They will fix the mines to the hulls of German ships in the harbour. And then they will paddle to the Spanish border, where French resistance fighters might be waiting for them, or might not.

Their commander is a Royal Marines major named Herbert Hasler. His men know him as Blondie. The submarine HMS Tuna surfaces off the French coast on December the seventh. Five canoes get into the water. The sixth is damaged on launch and stays behind.

Of the ten men who paddle into the estuary, two are swept out into the Atlantic in the first night and drown. Two are captured on the second night and shot the following morning. Two more are taken alive and executed in March. By the time the canoes reach the harbour at Bordeaux, only Hasler and one other Marine, Bill Sparks, are still attached to the mines.

On the night of December the eleventh, they paddle silently up to the German freighters and fix sixteen limpet mines below the waterline. Six ships are damaged. Two are sunk.

Hasler and Sparks abandon their canoes and walk. Through occupied France. They reach Spain. They reach Gibraltar. They reach London four months later.

Of the twelve Cockleshell Heroes who set out, two come home.

Lord Mountbatten, who approved the raid, said afterwards that of every operation Combined Operations Command ever conducted, none was more courageous or imaginative.

We are halfway through. Five raids to go. The first half were daring because they were small. The second half are daring because the consequences of failure were beyond anything most soldiers had ever been asked to carry.

Number five. Operation Gunnerside. Norway. The night of February the twenty-seventh, nineteen forty-three.

In nineteen forty, the Germans capture Norway. With it, they capture the Vemork hydroelectric plant in the Telemark province. Pronounced VAY-mork. The only facility in Europe producing heavy water in commercial quantities. Heavy water is what the German nuclear program needs to build a working atomic reactor. Allied scientists understand, very early, that if Vemork keeps running, the Germans will have a head start on the bomb.

A first British raid to destroy Vemork in November nineteen forty-two, called Operation Freshman, ends in disaster. Two gliders crash in the Norwegian mountains. The survivors are tortured and shot by the Gestapo. The plant continues to produce heavy water at four hundred kilograms a year.

So in February nineteen forty-three, the Special Operations Executive sends in a different team. Six Norwegians. All exiles. All trained in Britain by the SOE. They are dropped by parachute onto a frozen plateau called the Hardangervidda, the highest and emptiest mountain plateau in Europe.

They link up with four men of an earlier reconnaissance team who have been living off reindeer moss in caves for four months. They are now ten. Their commander is a twenty-three-year-old named Joachim Rønneberg. Pronounced RON-uh-berg.

To reach Vemork, they have to descend a six-hundred-foot ravine, cross a river that is half frozen, climb the other side, infiltrate the perimeter wire, and find an unguarded service tunnel into the basement of a fortified industrial plant. The Germans have decided that the cliff is impassable, so the cliff is not guarded. The Norwegians come up the cliff.

Inside the basement, they place plastic explosives on the eighteen heavy-water electrolysis cells. They set thirty-second fuses. They walk out.

The blast destroys five hundred kilograms of heavy water and every piece of production equipment in the plant. Not one shot is fired. Not one Norwegian is wounded. Not one German is killed.

They ski three hundred kilometers across the Hardangervidda to neutral Sweden, dressed in white, in the middle of a German pursuit involving three thousand troops. They reach safety. All ten of them.

Operation Gunnerside is the cleanest sabotage mission of the Second World War. It is also the single most consequential. The German atomic program never recovers. But before Gunnerside, in May nineteen forty-two, two Czech soldiers had jumped into occupied Prague to do something even harder.

Number four. Operation Anthropoid. Czechoslovakia. May the twenty-seventh, nineteen forty-two.

Reinhard Heydrich is, after Hitler and Himmler, the third most powerful man in the Third Reich. Pronounced HIGH-drick. He is the architect of the Final Solution. The chief of the Reich Main Security Office. The acting governor of occupied Czechoslovakia, where he is known to the locals as the Hangman of Prague. By nineteen forty-two, the Czech government in exile in London understands that as long as Heydrich lives, the Czech resistance inside the country will be hunted to extinction.

The British Special Operations Executive trains two volunteers. Jozef Gabčík, a Slovak. Pronounced GAB-cheek. And Jan Kubiš, a Czech. Pronounced KOO-bish. They are dropped by parachute into a field outside Prague on the night of December the twenty-eighth, nineteen forty-one.

For five months, they hide. They watch Heydrich. They learn that every morning he is driven from his country house outside Prague to his office in the city, in an open Mercedes, with no escort. He is so confident in the obedience of the Czech people that he believes an escort would suggest fear.

On the morning of May the twenty-seventh, the two men wait at a hairpin bend on the road. Heydrich's car comes around the corner and slows to make the turn. Gabčík steps out into the road and pulls the trigger of his Sten submachine gun. The Sten jams.

Heydrich, instead of ordering his driver to flee, orders him to stop, and stands up to draw his pistol. As he does, Kubiš throws a converted anti-tank grenade at the side of the car. The explosion shatters Heydrich's spine and drives splinters from the seat into his back. He dies eight days later, of sepsis.

The reprisal is unimaginable. The village of Lidice, suspected of harbouring the assassins, is burned to the ground. Every adult man, one hundred and seventy-three of them, is shot. The women are sent to Ravensbrück. Most of the children are gassed.

Gabčík and Kubiš, hiding in the crypt of the Saints Cyril and Methodius church in Prague, are betrayed. They die fighting eight hundred SS troops in the basement of that church for six hours.

The only successful Allied assassination of a top Nazi official in the entire war.

But Anthropoid was a killing. Number three was a rescue. And the man rescued was the dictator of Italy.

Number three. The Gran Sasso raid. Italy. September the twelfth, nineteen forty-three.

In July nineteen forty-three, the Italian king arrests Benito Mussolini. The Italian dictator is shipped from prison to prison around southern Italy to keep his location secret from the Germans. By September, he is being held in a hotel called Campo Imperatore, on the Gran Sasso plateau, two thousand one hundred meters above sea level in the Apennine mountains. The hotel can only be reached by cable car. There are two hundred and fifty Italian carabinieri guarding it.

The Italian government has just signed an armistice with the Allies. Hitler refuses to accept that Mussolini will be handed over to be tried. He orders his airborne commander, Kurt Student, to organize a rescue. Student gives the operational command to Major Harald Mors. Mors is given a Waffen-SS commando named Otto Skorzeny as a liaison. Pronounced Skor-TZAY-nee. Skorzeny will spend the rest of his life claiming he led the raid. He did not. But he is in it.

The plan is improbable to the point of absurdity. Ten gliders, each carrying nine paratroopers, will be towed to the Gran Sasso plateau and released directly above the hotel. They will land on the only flat patch of ground in front of the building, which the planners have measured from a single aerial photograph. They have been told the patch is two hundred meters long. It is, in fact, sloping, rocky, and barely large enough for one glider, let alone ten.

The first glider lands and breaks up on impact. The second slides to a halt fifty meters from the hotel doors. By the time the third has landed, the German troops are running across the meadow with submachine guns. Skorzeny crashes through the hotel doors, runs up the stairs, and finds Mussolini in his room.

Not a shot is fired. The Italian guards have been told that the German officers approaching them are official escorts.

Mussolini is bundled into a small Fieseler liaison aircraft, which manages, against everything that should be physically possible, to take off from a meadow at altitude with three men aboard.

A puppet state, the Italian Social Republic, is declared in northern Italy two weeks later. The war drags on another nineteen months.

But for sheer scale of audacity, only one raid in the Second World War surpasses Gran Sasso, and the British still call it the greatest raid of all.

Number two. Operation Chariot. France. March the twenty-eighth, nineteen forty-two.

The Normandie dock at the port of Saint-Nazaire is the only dry dock on the entire Atlantic coast of Europe large enough to accommodate the German battleship Tirpitz. As long as it exists, Tirpitz can be sent into the Atlantic to hunt British convoys, knowing she has somewhere to go for repairs. Without the Normandie dock, Tirpitz must operate from Norwegian fjords, where the Royal Navy can pin her down. The British need that dock destroyed.

Bombing it, in nineteen forty-two, is impossible. So Combined Operations approves the most ambitious raid in British military history.

A Royal Navy destroyer, HMS Campbeltown, has her bow packed with four and a half tons of high explosive set with delayed-action fuses. She will be sailed at twenty knots into the lock gates of the Normandie dock and rammed into them. She will then explode, hours later, while German engineers are inspecting the damage.

She will be escorted by sixteen wooden motor launches carrying two hundred and fifty Royal Navy commandos. Their job is to land on the docks while Campbeltown is wedged in the lock gates and demolish every other piece of port infrastructure they can reach. Then they are to fight their way through Saint-Nazaire to the riverbank and escape by sea.

Almost none of them do.

The Campbeltown rams the lock gates at one thirty-four in the morning on March the twenty-eighth. The commandos pour ashore and detonate every pumping station, every winding house, every fuel store within reach. The motor launches, made of wood and gasoline, are set on fire by German shore guns one after another. By dawn, the German garrison has cordoned off the survivors, and the British commandos surrender, out of ammunition, pinned in burning warehouses.

At noon, while German officers are touring the wreckage of the Campbeltown, the explosives in her bow detonate. The forward third of the ship vaporises. So does the lock gate. The Normandie dock will not be operational again for the rest of the war.

One hundred and sixty-nine men of the raiding force are killed. Two hundred and fifteen are captured. Of two hundred and fifty commandos, only five make it back to England on foot through occupied France.

Five Victoria Crosses are awarded for one night's work. More than for any other operation in the Second World War.

The greatest raid of all sent Tirpitz to the bottom of a Norwegian fjord. But number one saved more than two thousand civilians from being burned alive.

Number one. The raid on Los Baños. The Philippines. February the twenty-third, nineteen forty-five. Pronounced Los BAHN-yos.

By February nineteen forty-five, General MacArthur's forces have landed on Luzon and are pushing toward Manila. Sixty kilometres south of the city, behind Japanese lines, is the Los Baños internment camp. Inside it are two thousand one hundred and forty-seven civilians. Americans, British, Australians, Dutch, Canadians, Norwegians. Doctors, missionaries, businessmen, nurses, teachers, and their children. Some of them have been in the camp since January nineteen forty-two.

By the third week of February, two things are happening simultaneously. The internees are starving. Adults are surviving on six hundred calories a day. And American intelligence has learned, from an internee who escaped through the wire, that the Japanese garrison is preparing to massacre every prisoner in the camp on the morning of February the twenty-third.

The mission falls to the Eleventh Airborne Division. Two hundred and fifty soldiers from B Company of the First Battalion, Five-Hundred-and-Eleventh Parachute Infantry Regiment, will jump out of nine transport aircraft and land in a rice paddy directly outside the camp. At the same moment, a reconnaissance platoon, having infiltrated the area on foot the night before, will attack the guard towers from the inside. At the same moment, more than two hundred Filipino guerrillas of the Hukbalahap and the President Quezon's Own Guerrillas will block every road into the camp from the surrounding hills. At the same moment, fifty-four amphibious tractors will cross Laguna de Bay, a freshwater lake two kilometres wide, and pull up to the camp gate. After loading the prisoners, they will drive back into the lake and head for American lines.

If any one of these four elements fails, the Japanese garrison has time to begin the massacre.

The jump opens at exactly seven in the morning. The reconnaissance platoon hits the guard towers ninety seconds later. Within twenty minutes, every Japanese guard in the camp is dead.

Then comes the harder part. The internees, most of them malnourished, many of them children, must be loaded into the amphibious tractors. The Japanese have a full division at Lipa, fifteen kilometres away. Filipino guerrillas hold them off long enough to get the tractors loaded.

Every internee is evacuated. Two thousand one hundred and forty-seven people. Two American paratroopers killed. Two Filipino guerrillas killed. Six wounded. Not a single internee killed or seriously injured.

It would later be called a textbook airborne operation. It is studied at every paratrooper school on Earth to this day.

Most special forces raids in the Second World War succeeded in destroying something. Los Baños succeeded in saving everyone.

Ten raids. Ten missions. From a fortress that fell to gliders to a prison camp emptied by paratroopers and Filipino farmers in canoes. Most of these raids were fought by men who were paid the same as a sergeant in any other unit. Most of them never spoke about what they did again.

The Cabanatuan rescuers came home and went back to civilian jobs. The Cockleshell Heroes who survived were ordered, by Mountbatten himself, never to speak about Operation Frankton in public for decades. Joachim Rønneberg, the Norwegian who blew up Vemork, lived to be ninety-nine and was still giving school lectures the year before he died.

If these stories were worth your time, like the video. If you want to hear more of them, subscribe. We tell one of these every week, and the only reason we can keep going is people who watch all the way to the end. Like you.

Every primary source for this video is linked in the description below. None of what you have just seen is reenacted.

Next week, ten raids of the First World War. When the men did all of this without aircraft, without radios, and without satellites.

Until then. Thank you for watching.

ranks.title: Operation Chastise — The Dambusters
key_facts: RAF 617 Squadron, formed March 1943 specifically for the dam raid
Barnes Wallis's bouncing bomb (Upkeep) — drum-shaped, 4,000 lb, dropped at 232 mph from 60 ft
19 Lancasters launched the night of 16-17 May 1943
Möhne and Eder dams breached; Sorpe damaged
8 of 19 aircraft lost; 53 of 133 aircrew killed
~1,200 civilians and forced labourers killed in the floods
Wing Commander Guy Gibson awarded the Victoria Cross
ranks.unsolved_hook: The Ruhr was back online in months. The propaganda victory lasts forever.
ranks.connective_tissue_out: But Operation Chastise is only number ten. Because the next raid took a fortress no army had ever taken.

ranks.title: Fort Eben-Emael
key_facts: Belgian fortress completed 1935; considered impregnable
85 German Fallschirmjäger of Sturmgruppe Granit, commanded by Lt Rudolf Witzig (later Capt Walter Koch overall)
9 of 11 DFS 230 gliders landed directly on the fort's roof at dawn 10 May 1940
World's first glider-borne assault; first combat use of shaped charges (Hohlladung)
Belgian garrison: 1,200 men; surrendered after ~20 hours
German losses: 6 killed, 15 wounded; 780 Belgians surrendered
ranks.unsolved_hook: The blueprint every airborne unit on Earth would copy for the next eighty years.
ranks.connective_tissue_out: But the next raid proved a small force could rescue the people no one else could reach.

ranks.title: The Great Raid on Cabanatuan
key_facts: 511 Allied POWs liberated, 30 January 1945
121 men of US 6th Ranger Battalion + ~200 Filipino guerrillas (Capts Pajota and Joson)
30-mile infiltration through Japanese lines on foot
P-61 Black Widow night fighter used as airborne distraction over the camp
Firefight inside the camp lasted ~30 seconds
Casualties: 2 Rangers + 2 guerrillas killed; ~270 Japanese killed; 0 prisoners killed
Triggered by Palawan massacre two weeks earlier — 150 US POWs burned alive
ranks.connective_tissue_out: But before any rescue raid of this kind was possible, the British had to prove that a tiny force could capture something the Germans guarded as if their lives depended on it.

ranks.title: Operation Biting — The Bruneval Raid
key_facts: 120 paratroopers of C Company, 2nd Para Battalion, Maj John Frost commanding
Target: German Würzburg radar set on clifftop near Bruneval
Flt Sgt Charles Cox, radio engineer, dismantled the radar under fire
Components extracted: transmitter, receiver, display unit
Casualties: 3 killed, 6 wounded, 3 captured
Night of 27-28 February 1942
Recovered parts allowed British to jam the Würzburg system
ranks.unsolved_hook: A clifftop raid by one hundred and twenty men changes the air war.
ranks.connective_tissue_out: But the Bruneval raid succeeded because the men got in and out alive. The next raid did not. And the men who did not come back changed the war anyway.

ranks.title: Operation Frankton — The Cockleshell Heroes
key_facts: 12 Royal Marines (10 paddled), 6 wood-and-canvas kayaks (5 launched)
Maj Herbert 'Blondie' Hasler commanding
Launched from HMS Tuna 7 December 1942
100 miles up the Gironde estuary in five nights
Limpet mines fixed to German freighters night of 11-12 December
6 ships damaged, 2 sunk
8 of the 10 Marines died (drowning, capture, execution); only Hasler and Bill Sparks reached safety via Spain
Mountbatten: 'none was more courageous or imaginative'
ranks.unsolved_hook: Of the twelve Cockleshell Heroes who set out, two come home.
ranks.connective_tissue_out: The first half were daring because they were small. The second half are daring because the consequences of failure were beyond anything most soldiers had ever been asked to carry.

ranks.title: Operation Gunnerside — Norwegian Heavy Water Sabotage
key_facts: Vemork hydroelectric plant — only commercial heavy water producer in Europe
6 Norwegian SOE commandos parachuted onto the Hardangervidda
Linked up with 4 Grouse team survivors (10 total)
Commander: Joachim Rønneberg, age 23
Night of 27-28 February 1943
Climbed an unguarded 600-ft ravine; entered via service tunnel
Destroyed 18 electrolysis cells + ~500 kg of heavy water
Zero casualties; all 10 escaped — most across 300 km of plateau on skis to Sweden
Followed by 1944 sinking of SF Hydro ferry on Lake Tinn carrying remaining heavy water
ranks.unsolved_hook: Not one shot is fired. Not one Norwegian is wounded. Not one German is killed. The cleanest sabotage mission of the Second World War.
ranks.connective_tissue_out: But before Gunnerside, in May nineteen forty-two, two Czech soldiers had jumped into occupied Prague to do something even harder.

ranks.title: Operation Anthropoid — Assassination of Reinhard Heydrich
key_facts: Target: Reinhard Heydrich — chief of RSHA, architect of Final Solution, acting Reichsprotektor of Bohemia and Moravia
Operatives: Jozef Gabčík (Slovak) and Jan Kubiš (Czech), trained by SOE
Parachuted into Czechoslovakia 28-29 December 1941
Attack 27 May 1942 at hairpin bend in Prague-Holešovice
Sten gun jammed; Kubiš anti-tank grenade injured Heydrich
Heydrich died 4 June 1942 from sepsis
Reprisal: Lidice destroyed — 173 men shot, women and children deported, most children gassed
Gabčík, Kubiš, and 5 other paratroopers died fighting 800 SS in the crypt of Saints Cyril and Methodius church, 18 June 1942
ranks.unsolved_hook: The only successful Allied assassination of a top Nazi official in the entire war.
ranks.connective_tissue_out: But Anthropoid was a killing. Number three was a rescue. And the man rescued was the dictator of Italy.

ranks.title: The Gran Sasso Raid — Mussolini Rescued
key_facts: Mussolini imprisoned at Hotel Campo Imperatore, 2,112 m above sea level
Operation Eiche — 12 September 1943
Operational command: Maj Harald Mors; airborne commander: Gen Kurt Student
Otto Skorzeny along as Waffen-SS liaison; later inflated his role
10 DFS 230 gliders landed on a sloped, rocky plateau
First glider broke up; subsequent gliders landed within 50 m of hotel
Italian carabinieri did not fire — confused by Italian general Soleti accompanying the Germans
Mussolini flown out in a Fieseler Fi 156 Storch
Led to creation of the Italian Social Republic (Salò)
ranks.connective_tissue_out: But for sheer scale of audacity, only one raid in the Second World War surpasses Gran Sasso, and the British still call it the greatest raid of all.

ranks.title: Operation Chariot — The St Nazaire Raid
key_facts: Target: Normandie dock at Saint-Nazaire — only Atlantic dry dock for Tirpitz
Night of 27-28 March 1942
HMS Campbeltown — bow packed with 4.5 tons of explosive, fitted with delayed-action fuses
Rammed lock gates at 01:34, then detonated at noon while Germans aboard
16 motor launches, 250 commandos of No 2 Commando + RN demolitions
169 killed of the raiding force, 215 captured, 5 escaped overland to Spain
Normandie dock unusable for the rest of the war
5 Victoria Crosses awarded — most for any single operation in WWII
ranks.unsolved_hook: Five Victoria Crosses are awarded for one night's work. More than for any other operation in the Second World War.
ranks.connective_tissue_out: The greatest raid of all sent Tirpitz to the bottom of a Norwegian fjord. But number one saved more than two thousand civilians from being burned alive.

ranks.title: The Raid on Los Baños
key_facts: 23 February 1945
2,147 Allied civilian internees liberated (Americans, British, Australians, Dutch, Canadians, Norwegians)
Joint US 11th Airborne / Filipino guerrilla operation
B Company, 1/511th PIR — 250 paratroopers from 9 C-47s
Reconnaissance platoon hit guard towers from inside, 90 seconds after the jump
Filipino guerrillas (Hukbalahap + PQOG) blocked Japanese reinforcements from Lipa division
54 Amtracs (LVTs) crossed Laguna de Bay to extract internees
Casualties: 2 paratroopers + 2 guerrillas killed; 6 wounded; 0 internees killed or seriously injured
Internees were scheduled for execution that very morning
ranks.unsolved_hook: Most special forces raids in the Second World War succeeded in destroying something. Los Baños succeeded in saving everyone.
